title: Belbin's team roles
blurb: Name all nine Belbin roles in their three groups, recognise each from behaviour and use the model to balance a team.
question: A project team bursts with ideas and energy, but plans rarely turn into workable tasks and deliverables go out with careless errors. Using Belbin's model, what is the team missing and how should the project manager respond?

teach.body: Meredith Belbin found that the most successful teams were not those with the cleverest people, but those with a balance of behaviours. He identified nine team roles: patterns of behaviour through which people contribute to a team. Each role brings a behavioural strength and comes with an allowable weakness, the natural flip side of that strength. Most people have two or three preferred roles. A team role is not a job title.

teach.caption: Learn the groups: exam questions ask which group a role belongs to and which role is missing.

head: Role
Contributes
Allowable weakness
teach.caption: An allowable weakness is the price of the strength. Manage it; don't try to train it out.
Plant creates ideas, the Resource Investigator finds them outside the team, the Monitor Evaluator judges them.

teach.h: How a project manager uses Belbin
teach.caption: Understanding roles also reduces conflict: people see a colleague's weakness as the flip side of a useful strength.

teach.body: Kate maps her four-person team. Priya and Tom are both Shapers and keep clashing; nobody is a Completer Finisher, and the last handover pack was full of errors. Kate gives Priya and Tom separate areas to drive, asks Lena (a natural Implementer) to own a final-check list, and brings in the client's quantity surveyor, a strong Completer Finisher, to review documents before each handover.

teach.caption: Two Shapers (clash risk) and no Completer Finisher or Monitor Evaluator (gaps). Each person shows two roles.

teach.text: Belbin is about team ROLES (behaviours); Tuckman is about team STAGES (development over time). Don't mix them up. Also: a role is not a job title, people usually show more than one role, and a team does not need nine people. Older material calls the Co-ordinator 'Chairman' and the Implementer 'Company Worker'.

items: Each role has a strength and an allowable weakness.
The PM uses Belbin to build a balanced team, understand strengths, allocate work, spot gaps and reduce conflict.

summary: You can now name all nine Belbin team roles in their Action, People and Thinking groups, recognise each from behaviour and explain allowable weaknesses. You can also show how a project manager uses the model to build a balanced team, allocate work, spot gaps and reduce conflict.

A.q: In Belbin's model, which group contains the Shaper, Implementer and Completer Finisher?
A.why: Shaper, Implementer and Completer Finisher are the three Action roles.

whyNot.1: The People roles are Co-ordinator, Teamworker and Resource Investigator.
whyNot.2: The Thinking roles are Plant, Monitor Evaluator and Specialist.
whyNot.3: Belbin has no 'Support' group; the three groups are Action, People and Thinking.

A.q: A team member is calm and confident, clarifies the team's goals, delegates well and makes sure everyone contributes in meetings. Which Belbin role is this?
A.why: Clarifying goals, delegating and chairing so everyone contributes is the Co-ordinator.

whyNot.0: The Shaper drives and challenges with energy rather than calmly chairing.
whyNot.1: The Teamworker supports and smooths relationships but does not usually chair and delegate.
whyNot.3: The Implementer turns ideas into practical plans and gets on with the work.

A.q: What does Belbin mean by an 'allowable weakness'?
options: A skill gap that training must fix
A flaw found only in Plant roles
The flip side of a role's strength
A.why: An allowable weakness is the natural trade-off of a role's strength; it is accepted and managed, not trained out.

whyNot.0: Allowable weaknesses are part of the role, not gaps to be trained away.
whyNot.1: They are 'allowable' precisely because they come with a valuable strength.
whyNot.2: Every one of the nine roles has an allowable weakness.

B.q: Which TWO roles are in Belbin's Thinking group? 1. Plant  2. Teamworker  3. Monitor Evaluator  4. Implementer
B.why: Plant (1) and Monitor Evaluator (3) are Thinking roles, along with the Specialist.

whyNot.0: The Teamworker (2) is a People role.
whyNot.2: The Teamworker (2) is a People role and the Implementer (4) is an Action role.
whyNot.3: The Implementer (4) is an Action role.

B.q: A project team is full of energy and ideas, but plans never become practical, workable tasks. Which Belbin role is most likely missing?
B.why: The Implementer turns ideas into practical plans and actions.

whyNot.0: The team already has ideas; a Plant would add more ideas, not practical plans.
whyNot.1: The Resource Investigator finds outside opportunities, not practical plans.
whyNot.2: The team already has energy; the Shaper adds drive rather than practical planning.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Belbin's nine team roles?
B.why: There is no 'Project Controller' role in Belbin's model.

whyNot.0: The Specialist is a Thinking role providing in-depth knowledge.
whyNot.1: The Resource Investigator is a People role.
whyNot.3: The Completer Finisher is an Action role.

C.q: Two Shapers on a project team keep clashing as each pushes their own approach. How can the project manager best use Belbin to reduce this?
options: Give each their own distinct area to drive
Remove both Shapers from the team at once
Tell both to behave as Teamworkers only
Ignore it, since the conflict is allowable
C.why: Understanding both are Shapers lets the PM channel their drive into separate areas, reducing the clash while keeping their strengths.

whyNot.1: Removing both loses valuable drive; the model helps manage the overlap instead.
whyNot.2: People cannot simply switch off their natural roles on instruction.
whyNot.3: Allowable weaknesses are managed, not ignored; unmanaged conflict harms the team.

C.q: Belbin profiling shows a team has no Resource Investigator. Which risk does this most likely create?
options: Fewer checks for errors before each handover
C.why: The Resource Investigator explores opportunities and develops contacts outside the team.

whyNot.0: Objective analysis comes from the Monitor Evaluator.
whyNot.2: Checking for errors is the Completer Finisher's strength.

C.q: Which statement about Belbin's team roles is correct?
options: Each person shows only a single role
A team must always have exactly nine people
Roles describe behaviour, not job title
Roles are set by a person's job grade
C.why: Belbin roles are patterns of behaviour, independent of job title or grade.

whyNot.0: Most people have two or three preferred roles.
whyNot.1: A small team can cover all nine roles because people show more than one.
whyNot.3: Roles reflect behaviour, not seniority or grade.

reteach.title: Think of a pub quiz team
reteach.question: Why does a pub quiz team of four friends often beat a team of four professors? What roles is each person playing?

blocks.body: One friend blurts out wild guesses that are sometimes brilliant (Plant). Another weighs every answer before it goes down (Monitor Evaluator). One knows every football fact ever (Specialist). Someone keeps everyone calm when the round goes badly (Teamworker), someone decides whose answer goes on the sheet (Co-ordinator) and someone checks the spelling and hands the sheet in on time (Completer Finisher). Four professors who all think the same way lack that balance.

blocks.text: The roles are about how people behave in the team, not what they know or their job title. Balance across Action, People and Thinking roles is what makes the team work.

explain.body: Shaper: dynamic, challenging, drives the team through obstacles. Implementer: practical and reliable, turns ideas into workable plans. Completer Finisher: painstaking, searches out errors, polishes and meets deadlines.

test.q: Which Action role is dynamic, thrives on pressure and has the drive to overcome obstacles?
test.why: The Shaper is the challenging, dynamic role that drives the team through obstacles.

whyNot.0: The Implementer is practical and reliable rather than driving under pressure.
whyNot.1: The Completer Finisher focuses on detail, errors and deadlines.
whyNot.2: The Co-ordinator is a People role that clarifies goals and delegates.

explain.body: Co-ordinator: clarifies goals, delegates and chairs. Teamworker: co-operative, diplomatic, listens and averts friction. Resource Investigator: outgoing, explores opportunities and develops contacts outside the team.

test.q: What is a typical allowable weakness of the Teamworker?
options: Can be indecisive in a crunch
test.why: The Teamworker's wish for harmony can make them indecisive when a hard decision is needed.

whyNot.1: Being prone to provocation is the Shaper's allowable weakness.
whyNot.2: Reluctance to delegate is the Completer Finisher's allowable weakness.
whyNot.3: Ignoring practical detail is the Plant's allowable weakness.

explain.body: Plant: creative and imaginative, generates original ideas. Monitor Evaluator: sober and logical, judges options objectively. Specialist: single-minded, provides in-depth knowledge in a narrow area.

test.q: How does the Plant differ from the Monitor Evaluator?
options: Plant judges ideas; ME creates them
Plant creates ideas; ME judges them
Plant finds contacts; ME finds errors
test.why: The Plant generates creative ideas; the Monitor Evaluator weighs them up objectively.

whyNot.0: This is the wrong way round.
whyNot.2: Finding contacts is the Resource Investigator; finding errors is the Completer Finisher.
whyNot.3: Chairing is the Co-ordinator; implementing is the Implementer.

explain.body: The project manager uses Belbin to build a balanced team, understand each person's strengths, allocate work to suit them, spot missing or doubled-up roles and reduce conflict by helping people value their differences.

test.q: Which of the following is a way a project manager uses Belbin's model?
options: Spotting gaps in the team's role balance
Calculating each member's daily cost rate
Defining the critical path of the schedule
test.why: Belbin helps the PM see which roles are missing or doubled up so the team can be balanced.

whyNot.0: Development stages come from Tuckman's model, not Belbin's.
whyNot.2: Cost rates are a budgeting matter, not a team-role one.
whyNot.3: The critical path is a scheduling concept.
